items.title: Canada increases proof of funds for Nigerians, other foreign students
items.description: Canada has increased the amount of money international students must show when applying for a study permit, with the new financial requirement taking effect on September 1, 2026. Under the updated requirement, applicants must demonstrate that they have sufficient funds to cover their tuition, living expenses and transportation costs to and from Canada without relying on employment in the country. The financial requirement for living expenses is updated annually to reflect changes in the cost of living. For study permit applications submitted from September 1, 2026, students planning to study in any Canadian province or territory except Quebec must show C$23,448 for one person for one year, excluding tuition and transportation costs. The amount rises depending on the number of family members accompanying the student: One person: C$23,448 Two people: C$29,192 Three people: C$35,888 Four people: C$43,572 Five people : C$49,419 Six people: C$55,736 Seven people: C$62,054 Each additional family member: C$6,318 For example, a student travelling to Canada with two family members will need to demonstrate C$35,888 to cover living expenses for one year, in addition to funds for tuition and transportation. What applicants need to prove Applicants must provide documents showing that the required funds are available to them. They must demonstrate enough financial resources for the first year of their studies. Students enrolled in programmes lasting more than one year must also explain how they intend to finance the full duration of their studies. This could include evidence of a scholarship lasting beyond one year or proof that a parent is employed. Acceptable proof of funds can include tuition and housing payment receipts, student or education loans, scholarships, employment pay slips, letters from financial sponsors, Canadian bank accounts, guaranteed investment certificates and bank statements covering the previous six months. Applicants whose countries have foreign exchange controls must also demonstrate that they are permitted to transfer funds out of their country to cover their expenses in Canada. The post Canada increases proof of funds for Nigerians, other foreign students appeared first on Vanguard News .

items.title: Doufelgou/santé : Un atelier de cadrage pour renforcer la lutte contre les VBG
items.description: Niamtougou, 28 août (ATOP) – Un atelier de cadrage sur le projet de création et d’opérationnalisation d’un cadre de coordination multisectoriel et de mobilisation communautaire pour lutter contre les Violences basées sur le genre (VBG) s’est tenu le vendredi 28 août à Niamtougou. L’initiative s’inscrit dans la mise en œuvre des activités du Plan de développement communal (PDC) de Doufelgou 1. Ce projet se déroule sur trois mois (août en octobre) et bénéficie de l’appui financier la coopération allemande à travers la troisième phase du Programme Santé (ProSanté III) mise en œuvre par la GIZ. Présentation du projet Le but est de renforcer, de manière coordonnée et participative, les interventions dans les domaines du genre, de la lutte contre les VBG, de la santé sexuelle et reproductive, de la nutrition et de la santé communautaire. Il s’agit de rendre opérationnel un cadre de coordination multisectoriel réunissant les acteurs institutionnels, les organisations de la société civile et les leaders communautaires. Le dispositif prévoit des rencontres trimestrielles, la formation des leaders communautaires sur la prévention des VBG et les droits sexuels et reproductifs. Il concerne aussi la nutrition et la santé communautaire, ainsi que des actions de sensibilisation sur les normes culturelles néfastes afin de favoriser un changement durable des comportements. Des activités, entre autres, des campagnes de sensibilisation communautaire, des causeries éducatives, des débats publics et des sessions de renforcement de capacités sont prévues dans le programme. Des messages de prévention seront également diffusés à travers les radios locales, le théâtre-forum, l’affichage et les médias sociaux. La rencontre a permis aux parties prenantes de mieux appréhender le contexte et les enjeux du projet, mettant l’accent sur la nécessité d’une synergie d’action entre les secteurs de la santé, de la justice, des affaires sociales et de la sécurité. L’implication des communautés à la base devra également contribuer à déconstruire les tabous et à instaurer un environnement protecteur. Le maire de la commune, Massoka Barima, a relevé la persistance des VBG, des mariages précoces, des grossesses non désirées et de certaines normes socioculturelles néfastes, qui affectent particulièrement les femmes, les adolescentes et les groupes vulnérables. Selon lui, le projet entend contribuer à remédier au manque de synergie entre les différents intervenants sur le terrain. M. Massoka a exhorté les chefs traditionnels et les autorités locales à veiller au respect des futures dispositions, tout en appelant à un encadrement accru de la jeunesse. Il a également invité le conseil municipal à envisager des dispositions réglementaires visant à mieux protéger les jeunes et à promouvoir un cadre social sain. La rencontre a réuni des chefs traditionnels, des membres des comités cantonaux et villageois de développement (CCD et CVD), des représentants des confessions religieuses, des organisations de la société civile ainsi que des syndicats des corps de métiers. ATOP/SG/TAL/DHK

items.title: The Limits of Yayoi Kusama’s Infinity
items.description: Years before the polka-dotted pumpkins, before the Instagrammable Infinity Mirror Rooms, Yayoi Kusama made art that was charged with oppositional energy. Her performances, in which she painted dots onto the naked bodies of her collaborators, were an expression of ’60s counterculture. They were protests against the Vietnam War, rebukes to the art market. Her Accumulations—soft sculptures of furniture or common household items covered in stuffed, handsewn penis shapes—were hilarious critiques of phallocentrism and early examples of feminist art. Kusama was, in other words, part of the artistic avant-garde. Her death, at 97, is a cold reminder that the avant-garde no longer exists. You could point to Andy Warhol, Jeff Koons, Takashi Murakami, or Keith Haring, but in many ways, no one epitomizes the collapse of the avant-garde more vividly than Kusama. I’m mostly a fan of her work. It’s very hard not to like her Infinity Mirror Room installations and playful gourds, and not to smile when you see Kusama’s endearing face framed by her signature brightly colored bobbed wig. But at a certain point, you can’t help but feel that she stopped being an artist and chose instead to become a highly profitable brand. In death as in life, her name bestrides a tightly managed, commercially successful global enterprise with diverse revenue streams, including high-profile partnerships with luxury labels, licensed merchandise, and strictly managed intellectual-property protection. Kusama’s large-scale sculptures and immersive installations break attendance records at museums and galleries around the world, and her works regularly set records at auction. In her final years, she was one of the world’s top-selling contemporary artists. Decades before all of that, though, Kusama was a creative maverick. After moving to New York from Tokyo in the late 1950s, she became a pioneer of both pop art and minimalism, then a key figure in performance art. She called her early breakthrough paintings—expansive, swirling fields of tightly packed dots—Infinity Nets. Before even Andy Warhol (although after Marcel Duchamp), she made her own persona an expression of her art, paving the way for such figures as Gilbert and George, the British-artist duo who made life itself a performance. Seymour Wally / NY Daily News / Getty Yayoi Kusama paints Kent Feathergill in 1967. Kusama’s artworks had countercultural energy. They fought against cliché. They critiqued patriarchy. They broke down starchy inhibitions and wobbled magnificently on the edge of the rational. They tried, in other words, to open up new ways of seeing. That was what the avant-garde was all about: It was an attempt to see the world afresh. For many of its leading figures, from the Impressionists in the 1870s to conceptual artists a century later, this also meant proposing new and better solutions to the problem of how to be and how to live together. These proposals, many times rooted in sympathy and love, were presented as alternatives to the political structures and market logic that had so often led to war, exploitation, hopelessness, and suffering. Even when attempts to turn these imagined alternatives into reality failed—and often dismally—the avant-garde stood in a clear relationship to modernity’s traumas. It was like the whistle cap in the spout of a boiling kettle: both a release of suppressed pressures (psychic and cultural) and an alarm. But society got sick of hearing the alarm. And the kettle got tired of whistling. Kusama, having experienced a period of art-world success, had her own breakdown after returning to Tokyo permanently in 1973. Two years later, she checked herself in to a psychiatric institution, where she became a permanent resident from 1977 until her death. The institution was within walking distance of her multistory studio. [ Read: An artist for the Instagram age ] Her psychic travails had to do with her upbringing (she had an authoritarian mother and an unfaithful father), which left her afraid of sex and intimacy. She suffered from severe audiovisual hallucinations, in which she would see flashing lights, auras, and dense fields of dots. She fell into deep episodes of clinical depression and attempted suicide twice. When Kusama reemerged as an active artist in 1989, she and her supporters presented her mental-health issues not just as an important aspect of her personal story but as part of the energy that fueled her artwork. All of this was healthy frankness, but it also undoubtedly enhanced her work’s reception. People could relate to the idea of creativity as a function of—and therapy for—mental illness. Kusama and her promoters emphasized the link, tapping into narratives about the artist as a suffering visionary that went back to Van Gogh and even earlier artists (including such figures as Piero di Cosimo, Caravaggio, and Rosso Fiorentino) whose artistic brilliance was linked to their strange behavior and (perhaps) mental instability. In the 20th century, the idea of a connection between creativity and interior turmoil was taken up with renewed gusto, and the category of outsider art (or art brut) was established. Outsider artists could reconnect us to the amputated life of the emotions, re-enchanting a world diagnosed by Max Weber, in 1917, as disenchanted. Kusama was one of many artists who swam with these currents. She talked about her repeating dots as an expression of an inclination toward “self-obliteration”—an urge to dissolve into forever-expanding patterns. The idea sounded at once mystical, therapeutic, and nightmarish. The idea that it might be all three only increased her appeal. Christopher Furlong / Getty The immersive exhibition “You, Me and the Balloons” in Manchester, England, in 2023 This second phase of Kusama’s art-world success far surpassed the first, proving, among other things, that you didn’t need to be in New York for your career to go gangbusters. She became one of the most popular artists on Earth. For museums struggling with attendances, she guaranteed box-office bonanzas. Her zany, luridly wigged persona helped dismantle the intimidation factor that prevents many people from relating to art and museums. Her work’s upbeat vibes and instant recognizability (spotted pumpkins!) were huge factors in her popularity. They made it easy to let go of the idea that you had to have prior knowledge or be somehow “initiated” into art before you could enjoy it. Jim Dyson / Getty One of the artist’s Infinity Mirror Rooms in 2008 in Liverpool, England But the speed with which Kusama converted her popularity into massive commercial success was sobering, if only because it seemed to signal her total co-option by the market. A turning point came in 2012, when the luxury-goods brand LVMH, under the creative direction of Marc Jacobs, incorporated Kusama’s polka dots into its clothing lines, adorning stores all around the world with her designs. As Georgina Adam reported in her 2014 book, Big Bucks: The Explosion of the Art Market in the 21st Century , the collaboration caused sales of Kusama’s work to take off and exposed her to audiences she would have never reached otherwise. From that point on, Kusama’s absorbing and fresh art, once charged by avant-garde energies, became more or less a meaning-free expression of market principles, an exercise in branding. She soon became a social-media phenomenon—the world’s most Instagrammable artist. Crowds waited in long lines just to spend 30 or 90 seconds in her Infinity Mirror Rooms taking selfies. Kusama’s talk of self-obliteration sounds vaguely Buddhist or Taoist. But I suspect it’s more clearly seen, in the late phase of Kusama’s career, as pure capitalism at work—a function of the same logic relied on by Big Tech as it converts the liberating potential of the internet into addiction, polarization, and advertising revenue, and a drastic narrowing of human potential. You will no longer need an inner life , says this logic. You will no longer even be you. You will be data points and dollar signs. You will be ubiquitous, self-obliterating dots. Kusama also achieved something that has eluded other artists who were co-opted by commerce and converted avant-garde energies into branding, including Warhol, Haring, Koons, and Murakami. The artist—an adorable maker of giant spotted pumpkins who lived in a psychiatric institution—became beyond criticism. You could no more criticize her than you could a grandmother giving a teddy bear to an orphan. Chesnot / Getty The headquarters of the Maison Louis Vuitton in 2023 in Paris, France I have almost always felt delight when I’ve entered one of Kusama’s Infinity Mirror Rooms or encountered her pumpkins. But I smell something rotten behind their sameness and ubiquity. Successful branding is exactly what art at its best is not: a form of general seduction rather than specific engagement. I prefer the earlier Kusama, the artist of extraordinary boldness, who carved out thrilling new possibilities for art in a hostile, male-dominated field. For this, she paid a heavy personal price. But it didn’t stop her from making art that felt specific to her, art targeted directly at you and me.

items.title: Quelles sont les leçons de la guerre en Ukraine pour l’Armée populaire de libération ?
items.description: La Chine est un soutien clef de la Russie dans sa guerre contre l'Ukraine, en lui fournissant notamment des composants destinés à la fabrication de drones et en permettant l'utilisation militaire de biens à double usage, des technologies avancées essentielles au développement, à la production ou à l'utilisation des systèmes militaires. Mais l’Armée populaire de libération (APL) suit également de près le front. Cela fait en effet deux ans que des soldats chinois se forment au pilotage de drones et au combat urbain dans un complexe militaire de Volgograd, dans le sud-ouest de la Russie China is gaining troubling military know-how from Russia », The Economist , 23 juillet 2026.'> 1 . La Chine, qui n’a pas mené de réelle guerre depuis un conflit frontalier d’un mois avec le Vietnam, en 1979, cherche à compenser son manque d’expérience au combat en tirant profit de son partenariat avec la Russie. Pékin s'intéresse notamment à la lutte anti-drone menée par la marine russe en mer Noire, qui pourrait lui donner un avantage en cas d’invasion ou d'imposition de blocus naval autour de Taïwan. Une série d'éditoriaux récemment publiés dans le Quotidien de l'APL, le journal officiel de l'armée chinoise, suggère que Pékin a tiré plusieurs enseignements de la guerre en Ukraine. Dans un article publié le 16 août, un auteur appelle ainsi à « placer le développement de forces de combat anti-systèmes sans pilote au rang de priorité stratégique majeure et de le promouvoir de manière intégrée, en privilégiant la conception de pointe, les systèmes d'équipements et un entraînement au combat réaliste, afin de prendre l'initiative dans la guerre intelligente » 挑灯看剑丨把准反无人作战力量建设着力点 », 解放军报, 16 août 2026.'> 2 . Selon un autre auteur, l’essor de l’IA, du big data a donné naissance à « un nouveau paradigme », en faisant de l'innovation tactique le principal moteur de développement de nouveaux équipements. Alors que, durant les précédents conflits du XXe siècle, « les conditions matérielles et technologiques déterminaient les limites de la guerre », ce sont désormais les besoins tactiques qui dictent les spécifications techniques des équipements. L'armée ne se contente ainsi plus de « se battre avec l'arme qu'elle a », mais « fabrique l'arme pour la guerre qu'elle mène ». La majeure des enseignements tactiques abordés par les auteurs se concentrent sur l’utilisation de l’intelligence artificielle, de la rapidité du cycle d’innovation, de l’organisation des structures d’approvisionnement et de la collecte de données sur le champ de bataille. Selon l’Institute for the Study of War, l’APL considère la guerre en Ukraine « comme une phase transitoire de la guerre moderne » qui cédera la place à une guerre « intelligente », dominée par l’IA et les essaims de drones. La technologie a déjà fait l’objet de plusieurs essais en conditions réelles en Ukraine, avec le système « Pasika », développé par l’entreprise ukrainienne Sine Engineering. Celui-ci vise à permettre à un seul opérateur de piloter plusieurs drones simultanément, qui agiraient comme un escadron : un « essaim » pouvant compter jusqu’à 100 engins évoluant sur terre, en mer et dans les airs « comme une seule unité ». La Chine a déjà annoncé développer un « vaisseau-mère », le Jiutan , capable de transporter jusqu’à 100 drones sur une distance de plusieurs milliers de kilomètres au sein d’une structure alvéolaire. L’article Quelles sont les leçons de la guerre en Ukraine pour l’Armée populaire de libération ? est apparu en premier sur Le Grand Continent .

items.title: ‘Tinubu not an average politician’ — Duke rallies opposition for unity
items.description: The presidential candidate of the Peoples Redemption Party, Donald Duke, has urged opposition parties to unite ahead of the 2027 general election, describing President Bola Tinubu as a formidable political opponent who should not be underestimated. Duke, a former Cross River State governor, spoke in an interview shared by Symfoni, a podcast on its YouTube channel on Friday. The PRP candidate said the opposition would struggle to defeat Tinubu if political parties and their candidates remained divided, stressing that the advantage of incumbency gives the ruling party significant leverage during elections. According to him, the control of government institutions by the incumbent gives the president an edge that opposition politicians must take seriously. “Even if the APC did nothing, right? They’re the party in power. If there’s a problem on that day, the IG of police will not go to any of the contestants. He’ll go to the president. “So everything is skewed in favour of incumbent. Respect that,” Duke said. He argued that the opposition could only mount a credible challenge by setting aside individual ambitions and forming a strong coalition. “The only way you can seriously charge tackling incumbent is to come together to tackle and to have the force. “Otherwise, you’ll be factionalised. So, I think when you talk of rigging, we’re rigging it against ourselves because of our ego. We need to come together,” he said. Duke also warned opposition politicians against underestimating Tinubu’s political experience and strength, using an analogy to illustrate the difficulty of defeating the incumbent without adequate preparation. “Bola Tinubu is not an average politician. You don’t go to fight a lion who also has horns,” he said. Explaining his analogy, the former governor said an opponent with considerable political strength could easily overwhelm a fragmented opposition. “Can you imagine a lion with a horn? Yes, right? It’s already a dangerous animal. “Then you now give it a horn and you say go and fight it with knife and fork. You’ll be the dinner. So, let’s get real,” Duke said. He maintained that opposition politicians must recognise the realities of incumbency and work towards building a united political force rather than allowing personal interests to undermine their chances. Duke’s comments come as opposition parties and politicians intensify consultations and realignments ahead of the 2027 presidential election, with several groups exploring possible alliances to challenge the All Progressives Congress and Tinubu. As a presidential candidate of the PRP, Duke is himself among the opposition figures seeking the presidency in 2027. His call for unity highlights the growing debate over whether Nigeria’s opposition parties can overcome competing interests and establish a common platform capable of mounting a serious challenge to the incumbent. items.description: BURKINA -GOURMA -ASSAINISSEMENT-DESHERBAGE Gourma : Une quarantaine de membres d’associations assainissent la cour et la devanture du haut-commissariat du Gourma Fada N’Gourma, 27 août 2026 (AIB)-Une quarantaine de membres des associations « Tin Taani Fi » et « Yanyenma » ont bravé la pluie, le jeudi 27 août 2026, pour mener une opération de salubrité au Haut-commissariat de la province du Gourma. Les participants ont procédé au désherbage et à l’assainissement des locaux et de la cour du Haut-commissariat du Gourma. L’initiative a été saluée par le Haut-commissaire de la province du Gourma, Silas Nacanabo. Cette action d'assainissement a été conduite conjointement par l'association « Tin Taani Fi », dirigée par sa présidente, Noumpoa Tankoano, et l'association « Yanyenma », par son président, Yombo David Diakouma. Présent pour constater le déroulement des travaux, le Haut-commissaire de la province du Gourma, Silas Nacanabo, a exprimé sa gratitude aux participants pour cette mobilisation patriotique. L'autorité provinciale a vivement salué cet acte citoyen et a souligné qu'il permet d'offrir un cadre de travail propre et sain, au bénéfice des agents de l'administration et des usagers du service public. items.title: Décentralisation : La commune Bas-Mono 1 entame l’élaboration de son PDC
items.description: Afagnan, 28 août (ATOP) – Le processus d’élaboration du Plan de développement communal (PDC) de la commune Bas-Mono 1 a été lancé, le jeudi 27 août à Afagnan. Cette activité s’inscrit dans le cadre de la mise en œuvre du processus de décentralisation pour un développement local durable et harmonieux des communautés. L’objectif est de mobiliser la population pour leur adhésion au processus. Le PDC est un document stratégique, indispensable pour la planification des actions afin de promouvoir un meilleur cadre de vie et améliorer les services sociaux de base aux communautés. C’est un outil destiné à orienter les actions et les investissements de la commune au cours des prochaines années. La rencontre a permis aux différents acteurs impliqués de prendre contact et de mettre en place les différents comités spécialisés chargés de conduire le processus d’élaboration du PDC. Les travaux d’élaboration vont s’étendre sur une durée de 6 à 8 mois, au terme de laquelle, la commune disposera d’un cadre de référence permettant de mieux planifier ses priorités et ses actions de développement. A travers cette démarche, la commune entend ainsi se doter d’une vision concertée de son développement en tenant compte des besoins et aspirations des populations. Le 2 ème adjoint au maire, Faustin Akakpo a relevé l’importance du PDC qui permettra à la mairie de relever les défis pour satisfaire les besoins des populations. Il a exhorté les acteurs et les populations à s’impliquer davantage dans la mise en œuvre du processus en vue de son heureux aboutissement. ATOP /DK/BA

items.title: 'No oath, no membership': ECP withdraws notification for Senate by-poll on seat won by PTI's Murad Saeed
items.description: ISLAMABAD: The Election Commission of Pakistan (ECP) on Friday formally withdrew its April 2 notification for the by-election programme for a general Senate seat from Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which it had earlier declared vacant following the disqualification of PTI senator-elect Murad Saeed. In a notification, the ECP withdrew the election programme issued under its April 2 notification to “fill one general seat” in the Senate from KP, in pursuance of an order dated Aug 20. The withdrawal came a week after critics accused the ECP of assuming the role of a court by interpreting the Constitution to hold that no lawful vacancy had been created. Senate elections for 11 vacant seats from KP were held on July 21 last year. Saeed was declared a returned candidate for a general seat on July 24, 2025. However, on March 7 this year, Saeed was convicted by Rawalpindi’s Anti-Terrorism Court-I and sentenced to 10 years of imprisonment in the State vs Asim Rehman case, and on March 25, the commission determined that Saeed had been disqualified under Article 63(1)(h) of the Constitution. His seat was accordingly declared vacant. The by-poll was fixed for April 23 in the KP Assembly, but the process was halted after a petition was filed by PML-N MPA Jalal Khan, who argued that no lawful vacancy existed to justify the by-election. No oath, no membership, commission says In its detailed order, the ECP held that a clear constitutional distinction existed between a “returned candidate” and a “Member of Parliament”. “The publication of such notification signifies the conclusion of the electoral process to the extent of declaring a person as the returned candidate. However, such declaration, by itself, does not confer upon the returned candidate the constitutional status of a member of the Majlis-i-Shoora (Parliament),” the order states. Citing Article 255(3), the commission noted: “Where a person is required by the Constitution to make an oath before he enters upon an office, he shall be deemed to have entered upon the office on the day on which he makes the oath.” It further referred to Article 65, which bars a person from sitting or voting “until he has made before the House oath in the form set out in the Third Schedule”. The ECP noted the significance of the deliberate use of the expression “person elected” instead of “Member” in Article 65, saying that it demonstrated that “the Constitution itself recognises a distinction” between a person who had been elected or returned, and a person who had acquired the status of a member. Until the administration of the prescribed oath, a returned candidate remains a person elected to the House and does not attain the constitutional status of a Member,” the order reads. The ECP also interpreted Article 64 and Article 63(1) to mean that resignation or disqualification leading to a vacancy applied only to a person who had already acquired membership. “Therefore, the question of a seat becoming vacant arises only after the constitutional relationship of membership has been established,” it said. On Article 63(1)(h), the commission said clauses (g) and (h) “must be read in conjunction with the expression ‘from being a member’, as these provisions relate to circumstances where an existing member incurs a disqualification affecting his continuance in office”. The order concluded that a person could not be declared to have lost a seat which he had never occupied as a member, nor could a vacancy arise “in respect of a seat where the constitutional status of membership was never acquired”. “The commission is of the considered view that, notwithstanding the conviction of Murad Saeed, he has not yet acquired the status of a Member of Parliament; therefore, no lawful vacancy has arisen in respect of the said seat,” it said, adding that the question of holding a by-election therefore did not arise. Accordingly, the commission accepted the application and withdrew the April 2 election programme. Although the notification to withdraw the election programme after around five months is available on ECP’s official website, the order it was based on is not available.

items.title: Sebta : Madrid appelle au calme après les violences contre les migrants
items.description: « La violence n'est pas la solution » à Sebta, a plaidé vendredi le ministre espagnol de l'Intérieur Fernando Grande-Marlaska, après plusieurs incidents jeudi dans l'enclave espagnole qui a connu il y a un mois une entrée massive et illégale de migrants. Des scènes d'une grande violence alimentent la ville occupée de Sebta, où des nationalistes espagnols et racistes, se sont attaqués aux migrants et brûlé leurs effets personnels. « J'appelle au calme et à la cessation de toute forme de violence, car (…) la violence n'est pas la solution pour résoudre un problème aussi complexe » que celui auquel est confronté le petit territoire espagnol du nord de l'Afrique de 18,5 km2, a déclaré Fernando Grande-Marlaska au Congrès à Madrid. « Nul ne peut ni ne doit se faire justice soi-même », a aussi déclaré vendredi le président du gouvernement local de Sebta occupée, Juan Vivas (Parti populaire, droite), dans une déclaration solennelle, rejetant « avec la plus grande fermeté l'usage de quelque forme de violence que ce soit », tout en estimant « légitimes et pleinement justifiées les manifestations » qui exigent le « retour à la normalité » de l'enclave occupée. Près d'un millier de migrants sont entrés à Sebta les 30 et 31 juillet, et bien que la plupart soient repartis, une partie – 5.000 selon le gouvernement central de gauche, 10.000 selon les autorités de Sebta – demeure dans l'enclave occupée de quelque 80.000 habitants, errant dans les rues et dormant dans des camps improvisés ou sur les plages. Les manifestations des habitants de Sebta occupée, qui demandent leur départ et dénoncent des problèmes de sécurité, ont pris de l'ampleur et ont dégénéré ces derniers jours en violences contre les migrants. Jeudi, des heurts provoqués par des habitants de la ville, ont eu lieu sur une plage où campent des migrants, et leur effets personnels ont été incendiés. Le même jour, un soldat a été blessé lorsqu'un véhicule militaire a été attaqué à coups de pierres par environ 70 migrants, dont 12 Marocains qui ont été arrêtés. Deux autres migrants marocains ont été arrêtés jeudi également après avoir agressé un agent de la Garde civile, a confirmé vendredi à l'AFP une source proche de l'enquête. Vendredi, après ces épisodes de violences signés par les habitants de Sebta occupée, le Coordonnateur des organisations de développement et Amnesty International ont exprimé leur « profonde inquiétude », dénonçant la « dérive violente » et le « climat croissant de violence et de tension dans les rues » de Sebta contre les migrants dont plusieurs témoignages ont fait état de violences physiques de la part des agents de l'ordre espagnols. Les deux organisations ont appelé les autorités espagnoles à apporter une « réponse coordonnée » pour protéger les migrants et les réfugiés assurer la sécurité du personnel humanitaire et empêcher « l’exploitation politique » de cette crise, rapport l'agence espagnole Europa Press. « Amnesty International a pointé du doigt des organisations comme la Croix-Rouge », souligne la même source, en demandant qu'elles puissent mener à bien leur travail « dans des conditions sûres » et « sans crainte », après avoir constaté qu'elles subissent des « menaces » et que leur travail de distribution d'eau et de nourriture est « entravé ». Dans un communiqué, Amnesty International a noté et dénoncé l'incendie « en plein jour » et « en toute impunité » d'une partie du campement informel sur la plage de Benítez. L'ONG a affirmé avoir reçu des témoignages de « recours excessif à la force » par des membres des forces de sécurité espagnols et d'attaques commises par des individus accompagnées d'« insultes racistes ». Pour sa part, le Coordonnateur des organisations de développement a rappelé qu’il s’agit d’une « crise humanitaire » qui doit être traitée dans le respect des « principes humanitaires et du droit international ». Devant les députés, le ministre de l'Intérieur espagnol, Fernando Grande-Marlaska, a fustigé l'extrême droite et la droite, les accusant de diffuser de fausses informations, « de chercher à tirer profit politiquement de la situation ou, pire encore, d'inciter à la haine et à la confrontation entre personnes dans les rues de Sebta ». items.title: 2027: Group demands 5% APC campaign slots for Diaspora
items.description: ​By Femi Bolaji ​JALINGO — President of the Nigerian Community in Turkey and Chairman of the Tinubu Diaspora Support Group, Prince Emre Margboh, has urged the leadership of the All Progressives Congress (APC) to allocate at least five per cent of its 2027 presidential campaign structure to credible Diaspora representatives. ​Margboh, in a statement on Friday by his media aide, Acho Righteous, said the inclusion of credible Diaspora support groups would further enrich the presidential campaign structure. ​While congratulating the stakeholders who made the list, he stressed that their selection is a responsibility they must take seriously. ​He said: “I also commend Mr. President for directing that the structure should be inclusive and carry everyone along. ​”However, the Diaspora must also be carried along. Nigerians abroad are doing so much for this party and for our country. We are appealing to the APC leadership to consider at least five per cent representation for the Diaspora in the campaign structure.” ​Margboh noted that Nigerians abroad remain critical stakeholders contributing to national development and party growth through grassroots mobilization, direct foreign investments, advocacy, and humanitarian initiatives. ​Furthermore, he stressed that integrating Diaspora leaders into the campaign architecture would expand the party’s international reach and galvanize broader global support for the administration’s Renewed Hope Agenda. ​He charged party faithful across Nigeria and abroad to maintain discipline, foster unity, and prioritize the collective interest of the party ahead of the 2027 general elections. items.title: Gourma/Faso Mêbo : L’Entreprise Tienu Sela offre du carburant et de l’eau minérale à l’antenne régionale
items.description: BURKINA-GOURMA-CONTRIBUTION-FASO-MEBO Gourma/Faso Mêbo : L’Entreprise Tienu Sela offre du carburant et de l’eau minérale à l’antenne régionale Fada N’Gourma, 28 août 2026 (AIB)-Le Président-directeur général (PDG) de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela, Amos Djolgou, accompagné de son personnel, a fait un don de 100 litres de gasoil et de 30 packs d’eau minérale ce vendredi 28 août 2026 à Fada N’Gourma, à l’Agence Faso Mêbo. L'équipe a également participé aux travaux de confection des pavés. La mobilisation citoyenne autour de l’Agence Faso Mêbo se poursuit dans la région du Goulmou. L’Entreprise Tienu Sela a concrétisé son engagement civique à travers un appui matériel composé de 100 litres de gasoil et de 30 paquets d’eau minérale, destinés à soutenir les équipes de terrain engagées dans l’embellissement et l’assainissement de la ville de Fada N’Gourma. Au-delà de la remise symbolique de ce don, le Président-directeur général (PDG) de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela, Amos Djolgou et ses collaborateurs ont participé à la confection des pavés sur le site des travaux. « Je salue vraiment le président camarade, le Capitaine Ibrahim Traoré, pour l’initiative Faso Mêbo. Le travail que j’ai vu sur le terrain me réconforte très bien », a déclaré M. Djolgou. Il a salué l'action du coordinateur local et la propreté remarquable insufflée à la cité de Yendabili. Ce geste est la deuxième contribution de l’Entreprise Tienu Sela en faveur de cette initiative présidentielle. Au regard de l'impact des chantiers en cours, le premier responsable de l'entreprise a affirmé se préparer pour d’autres actions à venir. S'adressant aux citoyens, Amos Djolgou les a invités à visiter les chantiers de Faso Mêbo pour constater les réalités de terrain. « C’est notre pays, ce n’est personne d’autre qui viendra le construire à notre place », a-t-il rappelé. Agence d’information du Burkina KAC/HB/OO

items.title: Mali : une session spéciale d’examens de DEF pour les candidats de Kidal
items.description: a Kidal, 64 candidats au DEF, diplome d'etudes fondamentales, auront une nouvelle chance. Le ministere de l'education nationale prevoit une session speciale du 14 au 16 septembre, apres leur absence a la session de juin pour des raisons securitaires. Une nouvelle chance pour les candidats au DEF de Kidal. Le ministere de l'education nationale annonce une session speciale du 14 au 16 septembre 2026. Elle concerne 64 candidats de l'academie de Kidal qui n'avaient pas pu composer lors de la session ordinaire de juin, en raison de l'insecurite. Delocalisation des centres de Kidal lors des examens Les violences survenues le 25 avril dernier avaient provoque le deplacement de nombreux habitants. Les centres d'examen avaient alors ete delocalises a Gao et Menaka, mais la plupart des candidats n'avaient pas pu rejoindre ces centres. a Menaka, seuls 28 eleves sur 80 avaient finalement compose. Un cri de cœur attendu Face a cette situation, des organisations de la societe civile, ainsi que la Federation nationale de l'education, des sports, des arts, de la recherche et de la culture de Kidal, FENAREC-Kidal, avaient plaide pour une session speciale. Une demande desormais prise en compte par le ministere de l'education nationale. L’article Mali : une session spéciale d’examens de DEF pour les candidats de Kidal est apparu en premier sur Studio Tamani - Informations, débats, magazines : toute l’actualité du Mali, en 5 langues .

items.title: TPI de Kaloum : les trois leaders syndicaux de la BCRG renvoyés des fins de la poursuite
items.description: La décision dans l’affaire opposant le ministère public aux trois leaders syndicaux de la Banque centrale de la République de Guinée (BCRG) est tombée ce vendredi 28 août 2026 devant le tribunal correctionnel de Kaloum. Les prévenus, Aboubacar Sidiki Camara, secrétaire général adjoint du syndicat de la BCRG, Aboubacar Yansané, chargé de la santé, de la sécurité et de l’hygiène au travail au sein du syndicat de la BCRG, et Momo Camara, chargé des affaires sociales du syndicat de la BCRG, étaient poursuivis pour des faits d’« outrage à agent, violences et voies de fait », à la requête de l’adjudant-chef Daouda Sankhon, aide de camp du gouverneur de la BCRG, Karamo Kaba. Les faits remontent au 6 août dernier, lors d’un mouvement de revendication du syndicat portant notamment sur la prime scolaire destinée au personnel afin de contribuer à la scolarisation de leurs enfants. À l’audience de ce vendredi, le tribunal a déclaré les trois prévenus non coupables des faits qui leur étaient reprochés et les a renvoyés des fins de la poursuite pour délit non constitué. La juridiction a également débouté le ministère public ainsi que la partie civile de leurs prétentions. Dans sa décision, le tribunal a estimé que « les éléments constitutifs du délit d’outrage prévu par l’article 658 du Code pénal ne sont pas réunis à la charge des prévenus », et qu’il en était de même pour les faits de violences ou de voies de fait prévus par l’article 240 du Code pénal. La juge Fanta Alama Camara, qui présidait l’audience, a notamment relevé qu’« aucun acte matériel constitutif d’outrage ou de violence ou encore de voies de fait n’est établi ni personnellement imputable » aux prévenus. En conséquence, le tribunal a prononcé leur relaxe et débouté le ministère public de ses réquisitions. Sur l’action civile, la juridiction a également rejeté la demande de la partie civile qui réclamait le paiement de 100 millions de francs guinéens à titre de dommages et intérêts. Elle a aussi rejeté la demande de comparution des prévenus, faute d’éléments suffisants. Les dépens ont été mis à la charge de la partie civile. Cette décision met ainsi fin, en première instance, à la procédure engagée contre les trois responsables syndicaux de la BCRG. Elisa CAMARA L’article TPI de Kaloum : les trois leaders syndicaux de la BCRG renvoyés des fins de la poursuite est apparu en premier sur Mediaguinee.com .

items.title: Abia at 35: Orji Kalu put Abia in national conversation, made it punch above its weight — Chidoka
items.description: Former Minister of Aviation, Osita Chidoka, has described the administration of former Abia State Governor, Senator Orji Uzor Kalu, as a defining period in the state’s political history, saying Kalu put Abia firmly in the national conversation and made the state punch above its weight. Chidoka also observed that the momentum recorded during the Kalu era faded after he left office, with infrastructure deteriorating and Abia’s national standing diminishing in the years that followed. The former minister said Kalu understood the political realities that confronted Abia State and the South East at the beginning of Nigeria’s Fourth Republic and provided the assertive and visible leadership the moment demanded. Chidoka, who was guest speaker at the Abia State 35th anniversary celebration, stated this while reflecting on critical moments in the state’s history and the role of leadership in shaping its development and national standing. “At the beginning of the Fourth Republic, the South East was searching for voice and relevance in the new democratic order. Orji Uzor Kalu understood that moment. Young, assertive and politically visible, he put Abia firmly in the national conversation. Abia punched above its weight,” Chidoka said. His remarks offered a positive assessment of Kalu’s eight-year tenure as governor, particularly his ability to give Abia a strong voice and considerable visibility at the national level during the formative years of the Fourth Republic. Kalu, who assumed office in 1999, quickly became one of the most visible governors in the country and an influential voice on national issues. His political engagements extended beyond Abia, helping to draw attention to the state and the concerns of the South East at a time when, according to Chidoka, the region was searching for voice and relevance in the emerging democratic order. Chidoka contrasted the Kalu era with what followed, noting that the momentum eventually faded after Kalu’s tenure. He said infrastructure deteriorated, the state’s national standing diminished and Aba increasingly appeared to succeed despite government rather than because of it. “Over time, that moment faded. Infrastructure deteriorated, the state’s national standing diminished, and Aba increasingly seemed to succeed despite government rather than because of it,” Chidoka said. The former minister’s assessment effectively placed the decline after the Kalu era against the prominence Abia enjoyed at the beginning of the Fourth Republic, when, in his words, the state “punched above its weight” and was firmly established in the national conversation. He said the subsequent decline created another defining moment for Abia, adding that Governor Alex Otti appears to have understood the present opportunity to restore confidence in government, rebuild infrastructure and recover the state’s sense of possibility. “Alex Otti appears to have understood this one: a moment to restore confidence in government, rebuild infrastructure and recover Abia’s sense of possibility,” he said. Chidoka further argued that the debate over strong leaders and strong institutions should not necessarily present the two as alternatives, noting that societies at critical moments require leaders capable of building institutions that eventually become stronger than their founders. “We often say Africa needs strong institutions, not strong men. I agree that no society should depend indefinitely on one individual. But who creates strong institutions when the institutions themselves are weak? “Before there were the Ten Commandments, there was Moses. “My argument is that the real choice is not between strong leaders and strong institutions. At critical moments, societies need leaders with the capacity to build institutions that eventually become stronger than their founders. “The strongman makes himself indispensable. The strong leader builds a system that can eventually work without him,” Chidoka said. He said the challenge before Abia was to ensure that the current opportunity for renewal goes beyond an individual administration and develops into a lasting standard for governance and development. “Can the present Abia moment become the permanent Abia standard?” he asked. Kalu governed Abia State from 1999 to 2007 and currently represents Abia North Senatorial District in the Senate. items.title: After 30 years in service, I’m still waiting for my benefits — Lagos pensioner
items.description: Retirement has left Lagos pensioner, Michael Olawale Odesanya, confronting what he describes as a painful and uncertain wait for his retirement benefits after 30 years in service. In this interview with Damilola Ogunsakin, Odesanya speaks about the bureaucratic delays surrounding his gratuity and pension, the difficulty of meeting basic needs without a regular income, and the plight of other retirees, some of whom, according to him, have died while waiting for their entitlements. Tell us about your career in the local government service. I’m Michael Olawale Odesanya. I got employed into the Local Government Service Commission on July 4, 1996. So, when you add up from 1996 to 2026, that gives you 30 years. I was in the service for 30 years. I started as an Administrative Officer and ended as a Chief Administrative Officer, with various duty posts that I’ve administered. The last one being Administration and Human Resources. ‘Retirement From Lagos Service Is Like Terminal Disease’- Micheal Olawale-Wheelchair bound pensioner pic.twitter.com/kRVAYRUELQ — Vanguard Newspapers (@vanguardngrnews) August 27, 2026 How has retirement been for you? You know, it’s one thing to observe other retirees when you are in office, and at that time, you take it for granted. You begin to wonder, “How did this person get here? Why is this happening to him?” But now, I’m experiencing it. And I will tell you, retirement is like a terminal disease in this state. Because having been retired, it’s now open to me the number of other people who have retired who have not collected their benefits. And do you know the sadistic, ironic part of it? We run a PenCom system, that’s PFA, pension funds and so on. Each month, this outfit does not fail to deduct your contributions. You know, the civil service is one service where you don’t know the day you will enter, but the day you’ve entered, you know the day you are exiting, all things being equal, if you don’t die. So every other person, your employers know the day you are going. One will expect that automatically, you deduct the contributions. If we are humane enough, then we should prepare these things. If you can’t even meet the day of exit from the service, you should prepare ahead. How does this compare with the private sector? Private companies, you see the way they do their own. Once you’ve retired, maximum four months, you are called to get your benefits. I know NBL then, I know Spintex then, when they were at their peak. We had friends who were just factory workers; we had parents of friends who were just factory workers. The next year, “Ah, my daddy has retired.” Before three months, four months, that fellow got gratuity and things like that. So why should it now be government, the Alpha and Omega, treating retirees the way they are treating me? There are no exceptions. I’m just opportune that I have people like you to voice for the voiceless. How serious is the situation among retirees? If you wish to go by the way of pensioners and retirees who are dying, maybe two years, one year, six months after retirement, you’d be alarmed. And there’s nothing killing them because there’s no other way to go. Their last salary paid was in February. And of course, as a civil servant, you are not allowed to have any other thing doing strictly your job, right? Your pension, your PFA deduction goes every month. Your government gratuity is deducted and saved for you every month. So why is it now taking time to bring it out for you, the owner, knowing that it remains your sole source of livelihood after general work? Except maybe you are lucky, somebody drops your name, you are appointed, or you are enlisted as a political officer. Aside from that, how do we exist? How do we live? So it’s not been easy for me. What explanation have you received from the authorities regarding the delay in your benefits? They contacted me officially, saying I didn’t submit some documents, which is a lie. I’ll tell you that because I was HR. I ensured my documents were intact and taken to the commission. But then, that’s government. Everybody passes the buck. Bureaucratic bottlenecks - this is our major problem. So they sent it and said, “Well, I’ve not submitted these three documents.” Okay. As we speak now, I’ve submitted the three documents, and I have copies that were signed, attested to and acknowledged. So right now, I am waiting. Waiting is part of their cumbersome strategy. You could wait until Jesus never comes because most of them don’t feel like somebody is out there suffering, cannot eat, cannot survive without these things. They will tell you, “They are waiting for so-and-so approval.” Approval wo le n duro de? What approval are you waiting for? They said it’s in Abeokuta now. At the end of the day, let them just collect their entitlement, no matter how big, no matter how small. Just let them go. You have done yours. But no, I’m still waiting. I’ve submitted the requested documents. I’m waiting. How has the situation affected your health and ability to meet your needs? When you are with a disability, there are supplements you have to take - supplements, medicines. Most of these you don’t get in the general hospital. Most of the supplements I’m talking about, you don’t get them in the general hospital owned by the government. And most are imported. You have to place them on order. You get them by ordering them. Where do you have the money for such supplements now? There have been reports of pensioners planning protests over outstanding payments. What is your reaction? Generally, even those without disabilities, they are not finding it easy. If you’ve been following the trend, you will see that this coming week, maybe today or tomorrow, some pensioners are planning to storm Alausa. What is their grievance? They said our President, Bola Ahmed Tinubu, has paid backlog arrears, maybe going to over three months now. The President has released such monies, and somebody somewhere here is not thinking that people should get those arrears and get some soothing for the pains. Nobody just cares. What would you like the authorities to do now? We will not be restrained in any way. The last time it was Punch. Thank God today it’s Vanguard. If they delay too much, I might have to call an international world conference to expose what I believe is the injustice being done to vulnerable people because that’s the way it’s going to be. I want them to see this as a special case and so treat it specially, kiakia (immediately) Ogbe f’ohun f’olohun (Giving what belongs to others to the rightful owner). That’s what Ifa says. That’s it. items.title: Nigeria can cut oil production costs with local chemicals — Engineer
items.description: By Udeme Akpan, Energy Editor A Nigerian chemical engineer, Godswill Chidiebere Agomuo, has called for increased local formulation and production of specialised oilfield chemicals, saying the move could reduce operating costs, promote technology transfer and strengthen Nigeria’s technical capacity in the oil and gas industry. At an estimated average of about $40 per barrel, Nigeria’s crude oil production costs are among the highest in the OPEC+ group, far above the bloc’s roughly $10-per-barrel average. However, Agomuo, Technical Manager at Pacegate Energy & Resources Ltd (PEARL), who has more than two decades of experience in production chemistry, said locally formulated production chemicals could be effectively deployed across production platforms and flow stations while being adapted to the specific characteristics of Nigerian crude. He made the case while highlighting the importance of production chemistry and flow assurance to reliable hydrocarbon production. According to him, the continued reliance on finished, imported specialty production chemicals limits the development of indigenous technical capacity in the petroleum industry. “For many decades, the reliance on finished, imported specialty production chemicals in Nigeria has been a significant departure from the Federal Government’s resolve to promote credible indigenous participation in the oil and gas industry,” Agomuo said. “In my view, locally formulated and blended production chemicals can be developed and deployed effectively across production platforms and flow stations.” He said developing the capability locally would not only reduce dependence on imported products but also enable Nigerian engineers and service companies to develop solutions that respond to changing production conditions. “This approach has the potential to promote technology transfer while strengthening the technical capacity of Nigerian engineers and other industry professionals,” he said. “One of the key advantages of developing local formulation capability is that production chemicals can become more cost-effective and readily available to operators.” Agomuo further said locally produced chemicals could be modified to meet the changing requirements of individual oilfields. “More importantly, locally formulated and blended products can be re-engineered and optimised to meet specific crude-oil treatment requirements as field conditions and reservoir chemistry change,” he stated. His comments come against the backdrop of efforts by Nigeria’s oil industry to increase crude production, improve the performance of existing assets and deepen local participation across the petroleum value chain. One of the technical areas where production chemistry is critical is flow assurance, which deals with maintaining the reliable movement of hydrocarbons through wells, pipelines and production facilities. Crude oil contains different hydrocarbon components that can behave differently when temperature and pressure change. Under certain conditions, paraffin or wax can separate from crude and deposit inside production systems. Such deposits can restrict flow and create operational challenges, making the selection and application of appropriate chemical treatments important to maintaining production efficiency. Agomuo said the selection of an appropriate chemical treatment should begin with a detailed understanding of the crude oil. “The approach is simple, but it is fundamentally data-driven,” he said. “It involves integrating chemical engineering and chemistry principles from the initial laboratory evaluation. We first establish key crude-oil properties, including the wax appearance temperature (WAT), wax content and composition, API gravity, viscosity and the overall oil composition.” He explained that the information is subsequently used to assess available chemical formulations against specific performance requirements. “These parameters provide the basis for screening different wax-inhibitor, or pour-point depressant (PPD), chemistries against defined key performance indicators (KPIs),” he said. However, Agomuo stressed that laboratory performance alone cannot determine whether a chemical solution will work effectively in an operating oilfield. “The objective is to identify the best-performing product that meets the required technical KPIs. However, laboratory performance is only the first stage,” he said. According to him, the selected formulation must subsequently undergo field evaluation. “The selected product must subsequently be evaluated under actual field operating conditions to establish how it performs in the production environment before a final selection decision is made,” he stated. This approach is particularly important because conditions in operating oilfields can differ significantly from controlled laboratory environments. Temperature, pressure, crude composition, water content, equipment configuration, chemical dosage and production rates can all affect the performance of a treatment programme. Consequently, production chemistry involves more than simply supplying chemicals to an operator. It requires the identification of a specific production problem, laboratory analysis, formulation selection, field testing and continuous optimisation. Agomuo’s experience includes work on the re-engineering of paraffin-wax inhibitor formulations at Asharami Energy, where the objective was to improve flow-assurance performance while reducing chemical injection requirements. Such optimisation can have commercial implications because chemical treatment is a recurring operating cost for producers. Reducing the quantity of chemical required while maintaining or improving performance can potentially lower operating expenditure and improve the economics of production operations. Agomuo said Nigeria should therefore focus on developing local capabilities that combine chemical formulation with engineering and field knowledge. “Building this capability means that we are not simply manufacturing chemicals locally; we are developing the technical knowledge, formulation expertise and engineering capacity required to respond to the evolving needs of Nigeria’s oil and gas production industry,” he said. He argued that this would represent a deeper form of local content, moving beyond the procurement of locally supplied goods and services to the development of indigenous technology and specialised expertise. The engineer’s position also comes as Nigerian oilfield-service companies seek greater opportunities to provide specialised services to upstream operators. Agomuo has contributed to technical engagements involving ND Western and NDPR (Aradel), including multimillion-dollar contracts. His professional qualifications include registration and licensing as an engineer with the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN), as well as professional membership and licensing with the Institute of Registered Chemists of Nigeria. He said production chemistry and flow assurance should receive greater attention as Nigeria seeks to improve crude production and optimise existing petroleum assets. The future of production chemistry and flow assurance in Nigeria will be increasingly defined by our ability to develop indigenous technical expertise, local formulation capability, and innovative chemical solutions that support safe, reliable, and economically sustainable oil and gas production,” Agomuo said. He added that the disciplines should be regarded as strategic components of the petroleum industry. “In my view, production chemistry and flow assurance should therefore no longer be regarded simply as supporting functions within oil and gas operations,” he said. “They are strategic disciplines capable of directly influencing production reliability, asset integrity, operational efficiency, and the long-term competitiveness of Nigeria’s petroleum industry.” According to him, developing such capabilities locally would help Nigeria reduce dependence on imported technical solutions while creating opportunities for technology transfer and specialist skills development. “Developing this capability locally will be an important step toward building a more technologically independent, resilient, and globally competitive energy sector in Nigeria,” he said. items.title: Israel kills Hamas operative in rare West Bank air strike, military says
items.description: JENIN, West Bank, Aug 28 (Reuters) - An Israeli strike killed a Hamas operative and two of his accomplices in the West Bank on Friday, the military said, in a rare use of deadly air power in the occupied territory. Hamas confirmed the man that Israel named as Qais Bitawi was one of its members and condemned the attack that killed him. The allied Islamic Jihad militant group also claimed him as a member. The air strike targeted a car in the area of Jenin in the northern West Bank, the Israeli military and medics said.
